The one that is at the comparative lower order between any two ions in the series will donate an electron earlier and discharge or be oxidized. Between $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ and $\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{Cl}^-$ is situated lower than the other. So, $\text{Cl}^-$ will donate an electron earlier and be discharge or be oxidized. $\text{OH}^-$ is at the lower order between $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{OH}^-$. So $\text{OH}^-$ will discharge, donating an electron first and be oxidized.

**(ii) Effect of Concentration of Cations and Anions:** When there are more than one cations and anions in the solution, the effect of molarity is a more important factor than the tendency to discharge. The molarity of $\text{Cl}^-$ ion in $0.1$ molar $\text{NaCl}$ solution at room temperature will be $0.1$ molar. On the other hand, ionizing water, the molarity of $\text{OH}^-$ ion will be $10^{-7}$ molar. That means the molarity of $\text{Cl}^-$ ion is $10^6$ times larger than that of $\text{OH}^-$ ion. According to the electrochemical series, $\text{OH}^-$ is situated lower than $\text{Cl}^-$ and it is supposed to be the first to discharge. But due to molarity or concentration, $\text{Cl}^-$ ion in this case will be the first to discharge.

**(iii) Nature of Electrode:** Sometimes, the kind of electrode causes an exception in the above two factors of discharge in an electrolytic cell. $\text{NaCl}$ aqua solution has two kinds of cations- $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{H}^+$. When a platinum electrode is used, then according to the factor (i), $\text{H}^+$ discharges and produces $\text{H}_2$ gas. But this changes when mercury is used as a cathode and then $\text{Na}^+$ ion discharges earlier.

### Electrolysis of Pure Water

In the electrolysis of pure water, anodes and cathodes of some inert metals are used in electrolytic cells. Usually it is platinum. Water exists a little bit ionized:

$$4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{OH}^-$$
